rv.q: For what is clearly one of the past decade’s most loved plays, this Broadway debut is a beautiful homecoming.
Bioh, perfectly assisted by her sympatico director Whitney White and a no-weak-link cast, has done something quite amazing with this comedy-drama.
Jocelyn Bioh's sensational play, "School Girls; or, the African Mean Girls Play," captures this magic and anguish, set against the specificity of mid-1980s Ghana.
The show now possesses a spirit so exuberant as to enthrall for its joyous 80 minutes of running time.
White’s production understands this in a way that the show’s first New York run didn’t quite access.
Jocelyn Bioh’s breakthrough 2017 play about cliques and colorism is just as funny — and devastating — with a sharp ensemble and direction by Whitney White.
It’s a pleasure to be reunited with flawed, fractious but ultimately endearing classmates of this crowd-pleasing play.
Ms. Bioh’s sentimental but satisfying comedy is set in a private school in Ghana in 1986.
Deeply funny, exceptionally smart, and impeccably staged, this School Girls earns top honors.
Bioh once again enlivens a serious argument with abundant laughter.
School Girls is a comedy you won’t want to miss.

Benton and Rogers—each a radiant presence with resting Disney Princess Face—are perfectly matched rivals. As Paulina, Benton is unflinchingly cruel. She even draws gasps for her especially barbed comments toward Nana (Morton, hilarious and heartbreaking), her most amenable sidekick who’s grateful for the warmth of Paulina’s ambient light.
It will have you literally crying with laughter.
Every element of this top-of-its-class production has combined to make the production a true crowd-pleaser.
School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play has lost none of its sharp comic bite.
School Girls is uproarious, affecting, human, and sympathetic, too.
Bioh’s clever play employs the basic template of a queen bee making life miserable for her classmates to explore themes of racism, colorism, sexism, and self-destructive behavior.
Bitingly witty, this smartly constructed comedy transports us to the Aburi Girls Boarding School in 1986. Ghana.
School Girls; or, the African Mean Girls Play has some moments of bitterly divisive meanness but, with its plentiful laughs and tears, it’s also uplifting, unifying, and funny.
It’s elevated by delightful performances throughout.
But it also somehow feels slighter than it did when I saw it in 2017.
Unfortunately, these nasty encounters in “School Girls” are also far less witty.
Jocelyn Bioh's pageant comedy lands its laughs and its reckoning with colorism in equal measure.

School Girls or, The African Mean Girls Play...goes beyond the standard tropes of high schoolers being nasty about classmates' clothes, grades, or lack of cool to raise more profound questions about values, beauty, and prejudice.
Jocelyn Bioh is a very gifted writer in her ability to make piercing, biting, scathing observations about the world rolled into a comedic context.
“School Girls; Or the African Mean Girls Play” offers answers that cut deeper than the title suggests.
The piece has a big heart and effervescent buoyancy, but its message is clear.
Where the production shines is in the comedic set pieces, including a hilariously off-kilter rendition of a Whitney Houston ballad that allows each of the schoolgirls a moment to shine.
Buoyed by across-the-board terrific performances and Whitney White ’s enthusiastic direction, this entertaining trip to Africa via the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre is worth the price of passage.
The specificity keeps it from ever feeling boring, and the sharp barbs of bitchy dialogue and pearl-clutching moments of intrigue are instantly memorable.

cn.t: Critics praise this exuberant Broadway revival of Bioh's comedy about Ghanaian schoolgirls, citing Whitney White's inspired direction and sharp performances that elevate a predictable but funny script exploring colorism and teen cruelty with cultural specificity.

dr.inst: Available through the TodayTix app. Limit 2 tickets per person.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.

vr.q: Go see it with this stellar cast, great direction. Go see it on Broadway.
